newsitem.title: GERMANY: RWE stock surges on share rejig plan.
newsitem.headline: RWE stock surges on share rejig plan.

text.p: News that German diversified utility RWE AG plans to abolish multiple voting rights on shares mainly held by local municipalities sent the group's shares surging to new highs on Thursday.

The company's move to scrap the municipalities' rights, long viewed as an obstacle to institutional and private investors seeking to buy RWE shares, drove RWE stock to a new high of 88.30 marks in trade on the IBIS DAX index.

RWE shares were up 7.95 marks or 9.98 percent at 87.60 marks, while preference shares in the group were up 8.60 marks or 12.99 percent at 74.80 marks and heavy interest in RWE saved the overall market from dramatic losses.

The announcement prompted analysts to reassess the company. BHF Bank raised its recommendation on the stock to "buy" from "hold" and upped its EPS (earnings per share) outlook to 3.75 marks from 3.45 marks for 1997/98.

As it stands, Essen-based RWE has over 200,000 shareholders, but 60 percent of the voting rights lie with a group of 60 shareholders, who hold only 30 percent of the base capital with a value of around 2.8 billion marks.
The municipalities built up their voting rights over the years, as many are large customers of the utility group.

Their shares carry a 20-for-one voting right, which gives the communal shareholders the majority say. This system, which dates from 1924, has long irritated international shareholders, who view it as a relic of the old days.

The increasing globalisation of the German utility sector has left RWE's voting rights scenario looking increasingly anachronistic and RWE senior management has been trying for a number of years to update the shareholding structure to meet international requirements.
This pressure has combined with pressure from the Bonn government, which analysts say is preparing to do away with the majority voting rights system in imminent reform of German equity law.
RWE said on Wednesday that it planned to convert the registered common stock, with additional voting rights, into bearer common shares carrying standard voting rights.

Because voting rights would become available as a result of this move, RWE said holders of preferred shares would be given the option of swapping their shares for common shares with standard voting rights.
The holders of majority voting rights have previously called for compensation for handing over their rights, but Bonn is against payouts as part of its stated aim of scrapping the rights system.
RWE said the total number of votes would not change as a result of these measures.
The conversion of preferred shares would take place on a voluntary basis at a cost which had not yet been calculated.
The payments would be transferred to holders of registered shares to compensate them for the loss of additional voting rights, RWE said.
The cost of conversion would be calculated on the basis of the average long-term price differential between RWE's preferred and common stock.
RWE said it was inviting its shareholders in the public sector, the holders of most of its registered shares, to start negotiations on the proposal.
